title: Meeting Stravinsky in Germany; his guiding composers
summary: Stravinsky visited a rehearsal in Germany; Sauter names the composers who guide him.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Listening to classical music, then and now

blocks.x: So the one time that you spoke of that you met Bartok, that was your only face to face meeting with him?
Yes, but it was like meeting God.
I met Stravinsky once, not under similar circumstances; it was when he was--I
had a job at a German radio station in '57 and he was over rehearsing to perform, Agon, and they brought him into our rehearsal. Unfortunately I'm the conductor.
Most everybody in the band ignored me which was fine, because I expected that.
He hated conductor, he hated all the pretentions of conductors.
Hans Rosbog was the symphony conductor and he didn't treat him that well either.

We used to eavesdrop on the rehearsals; a wonderful conductor, that guy. I don't know what the exchange had been, but Rosbog walked down and presents the stick and said, would you like to. I said no, no. He said it was important to do it such a way.
The two of them had been my guiding lights. I still study, trying to

find out what's going on, along with Beethoven and Mozart; they never pay off. Some of the others do, but not those. Prokofiev is another one that stays there with me, and a lot of people don't think so, but I do. Debussy.

Nobody has really come along like that. They represent a cultural something that no longer exists and they could do it because their culture was a certain way and I think we're not producing that sort of genius because it takes time to gather up; something new is happening all the time now. Either that, or everybody is too much on the make today. I really don't know.
